passage: Hemant, you asked why my cousin Chiku actually listens to me? Okay. I'm Raghav, twenty, and I've been looking after Chiku, who's four, every evening since my aunt started night shifts. The first week was chaos. He wanted everything now: biscuits now, park now, cartoons now. So I started two things. One: I only promise what I'll definitely do. If I say "park after dal-rice," we go to the park after dal-rice, even if it's drizzling. Two: when he has to wait, we sing the train song, and every verse is one station closer. Last night he wanted ice cream from the freezer and I said, "After your bath." He sang all the way through the bath. Then he said, "Now?" And I gave it to him. That's it. That's the whole trick.

qa.q: What song do Raghav and Chiku sing while waiting?
qa.a: The train song, where every verse is one station closer.

qa.q: Why might Chiku be willing to wait now when he wasn't in the first week?
qa.a: Raghav's promises always come true, so waiting feels safe to him, and the song gives him something to do meanwhile.

qa.q: Which of Raghav's two rules matters most, and why?
qa.a: Only promising what will definitely happen, even the park in drizzle, because it teaches Chiku that waiting actually pays off.

qa.q: How might Chiku's mother, working night shifts, feel about this routine?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and grateful that her son is calm, cared for and learning to wait while she works.

grounding: A young caregiver explains how keeping small promises and singing while waiting taught a small cousin to wait.

passage: I'm Alka, doing my teaching practice at the same nursery school as Bhupen. The children in his group used to grab: crayons, the swing, the snack box. What I noticed about Bhupen is how carefully he keeps tiny promises. If he says, "You'll get the red crayon after Meena," he watches and hands it over the moment Meena finishes. He never forgets. And when a child is waiting, he counts slowly with them on their fingers, or they sing the "wait, wait, little star" song he made up. At first the children fidgeted. By the fourth week, I saw little Ravi standing by the swing, counting to twenty under his breath, not pushing anyone. When his turn came, he looked at Bhupen as if to say, "See? It works."

qa.q: What was little Ravi doing by the swing in the fourth week?
qa.a: He was counting to twenty under his breath, not pushing anyone.

qa.q: What does Ravi's look at Bhupen suggest he felt when his turn came?
qa.a: He seemed proud and pleased, as if he had discovered that waiting really does lead to his turn.

qa.q: Why do Bhupen's small kept promises matter so much?
qa.a: Because he always hands over the crayon or swing as promised, the children learn that waiting pays off, so they are willing to try.

qa.q: How has Bhupen's group changed from Alka's point of view?
qa.a: Alka has seen children who used to grab start counting and waiting their turn within four weeks.

grounding: A fellow trainee watches a young teacher keep tiny promises and model waiting through counting and song.

passage:
Week one: Harsha, home for the college break, told little Gargi, "Later we'll make paper boats," and forgot. Gargi cried. The next day, when Harsha said "wait five minutes", she screamed and grabbed.
Week two: Harsha started writing promises on a small chalkboard by the door: "Boats after lunch." After lunch, they made boats, every time. When Gargi had to wait, Harsha taught her to count the steps on the staircase, up and down, slowly.
Week four: On the last morning of the break, Gargi asked for the swing. Harsha said, "After I pack." Gargi went to the staircase and started counting, fourteen up, fourteen down. When Harsha came out with the bag, Gargi was already waiting at the swing, calm, holding out the rope.

qa.q: What did Harsha write on the chalkboard by the door?
qa.a: Promises, like "Boats after lunch."

qa.q: Why did Gargi scream and grab in week one?
qa.a: Harsha had forgotten the paper-boat promise, so 'wait five minutes' didn't feel trustworthy to her.

qa.q: What two changes did Harsha make, and how did they work together?
qa.a: Keeping every written promise and teaching Gargi to count the stairs; reliability made waiting worth it and counting made it bearable.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel finding Gargi calm at the swing in week four?
qa.a: Harsha would likely feel proud and relieved, seeing that keeping promises and teaching the counting game had helped Gargi learn to wait.

grounding: Over a college break, a young adult learns to keep small promises and teaches a little girl to wait by counting stairs.

passage: Shankar, you're worried about minding your little nephew for the whole vacation. Let me tell you something from when I was a young man of twenty-one, a brand-new teacher at the village school near Dharwad. I'm Darshan; the children called me Darshan Sir. My class of five-year-olds grabbed everything: chalk, the one swing, each other's tiffins. I'd say "wait" and they'd howl. So I made myself one rule: never promise what I couldn't keep. If I said, "After the song, you get the swing," then after the song, you got the swing. Every time. And I taught them a waiting song, counting to twenty on their fingers. By the monsoon, little Basavaraj, who used to bite, would hum the count under his breath and wait his turn. They learned waiting pays because I paid, every single time.

qa.q: What did little Basavaraj do by the monsoon?
qa.a: He would hum the count under his breath and wait his turn.

qa.q: Why did the children howl when young Darshan said 'wait'?
qa.a: At first 'wait' probably sounded like 'never' to them; they had no reason yet to trust that a later turn would really come.

qa.q: What choice did Darshan make that changed the classroom?
qa.a: He made a rule never to promise what he couldn't keep and paired it with a counting song, so every wait ended as promised and felt manageable.

qa.q: How might Shankar use this story with the nephew during the vacation?
qa.a: Shankar could keep small promises exactly and give the nephew a song or count to hold onto, so the child learns that waiting with Shankar pays off.

grounding: An elder recalls being a young teacher who kept every small promise and taught a counting song, building children's ability to wait.

passage: The bus to the clinic was forty minutes late, and the stop in Nagpur had no shade. Ramesh, four, tugged at his mother's dupatta. "Banana now!" Yamini was twenty-two and tired herself, but she crouched to his height. "When the bus comes and we sit, you get the banana. I promise." She held up her fingers. "Let's count red scooters. One... two..." Ramesh counted with her, then sang the train song, then counted again. Twice he whined. Twice she said the same words: "On the bus. Promise." When the bus finally lurched up, the first thing she did after they sat down was peel the banana. Ramesh ate it slowly, grinning. Last week she had done the same with the swing, and the week before with the storybook.

qa.q: How late was the bus to the clinic?
qa.a: The bus was forty minutes late.

qa.q: Why might Yamini peel the banana as the very first thing after sitting down?
qa.a: She wants Ramesh to see the promise kept at once, knowing that his trust in her word is what makes the next wait possible.

qa.q: Which of Yamini's choices at the stop helped Ramesh most, and why?
qa.a: Repeating the same clear promise and turning the wait into counting scooters; the words never changed, and counting gave Ramesh something to do besides wanting 🙂

qa.q: What is waiting like for Ramesh because of the past weeks with the swing and the storybook?
qa.a: Ramesh has seen his mother's promises come true before, so 'on the bus' sounds believable to him and his whining settles more quickly.

grounding: A young mother keeps small promises and turns waiting into counting and singing, teaching her child that waiting pays.

passage: Mehak was twenty-one and in her first month as a trainee at a nursery in Bandra. Little Kavitha, four, could not wait for anything. If snack was in five minutes, she cried. If the swing was taken, she pushed. So Mehak started small. 'After this song, you get the swing. I promise.' Then she sang the whole song, with Kavitha counting the verses on her fingers, and when it ended, Mehak took her to the swing. Every time. When snack was late, they counted to twenty together, loud and silly. If Mehak said 'after lunch', it was after lunch, never later. By the end of the month Kavitha could wait through a whole song without crying, humming along. One day Mehak heard her tell another child, 'Wait, wait. Mehak Didi always comes.'

qa.q: What did Kavitha count on her fingers?
qa.a: She counted the verses of the song.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha say 'Mehak Didi always comes'?
qa.a: Kavitha had come to trust Mehak because every small promise was kept, so waiting no longer felt frightening.

qa.q: What did Mehak do that built Kavitha's ability to wait?
qa.a: She kept every small promise exactly and gave Kavitha a way to wait by singing and counting together.

qa.q: How might Mehak feel hearing Kavitha say that?
qa.a: Mehak would likely feel moved and proud that her reliability had taught Kavitha that waiting pays.

grounding: A young nursery trainee keeps small promises and teaches a child to wait by singing and counting, and the child learns waiting pays.

passage:
'I want the ice cream now!' Baljeet stamped his foot.
'After dinner,' Pallavi said. 'I promise.'
'You'll forget.'
'Did I forget the park on Saturday?'
Baljeet thought. 'No.'
'Did I forget the story last night?'
'No.'
'So, after dinner. Want to count the minutes with me?'
'That's too many.'
'Then let's sing the train song three times. That's dinner time.'
'Three times?'
'Choo choo, off we go. One.'
Baljeet sang, grumbling, then louder. By the third song, the dal was on the table. He ate fast. Then he looked at Pallavi.
'Ice cream,' she said, and opened the freezer. 'See? After dinner.'
Baljeet licked the spoon. 'Didi, you always remember.'
'Always,' said Pallavi. 'That's the deal.'

qa.q: What song did they sing while waiting?
qa.a: They sang the train song three times.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet say 'You'll forget'?
qa.a: He was impatient and worried the promise wouldn't be kept, so waiting felt risky.

qa.q: How did Pallavi help Baljeet wait?
qa.a: She reminded him of promises she had kept, like the park and the story, and gave him a way to wait by singing the train song.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel when Baljeet says 'you always remember'?
qa.a: Pallavi would likely feel warm and proud that her reliability is teaching him that waiting pays.

grounding: An older sister caring for her little brother keeps her promises and helps him wait with a song, teaching that waiting pays.

passage: When I started coaching the under-tens at the colony ground last year, I made promises casually. 'Bowl well and you'll bat next.' Then time ran out and they didn't. I noticed Tanvir, eight, stopped waiting his turn. He'd grab the bat, sulk, walk off. At first I thought he was just impatient. Then I remembered: I'd broken my 'you'll bat next' three times with him. Why would he wait? So I changed. I only promised what I could keep. 'Three overs of fielding, then you bat.' And I kept it, every time, even when practice ran late. While they waited, we counted balls aloud or sang the silly boundary song. By March, Tanvir stood at the edge with his pads on, counting under his breath. 'Darshan Bhaiya, two more balls,' he'd say. He believed me.

qa.q: What did Darshan start promising instead?
qa.a: He started promising, 'Three overs of fielding, then you bat.'

qa.q: What did Darshan realise about Tanvir's impatience?
qa.a: Darshan felt a pang of guilt, realising Tanvir had no reason to wait after three broken promises.

qa.q: What changed Tanvir's ability to wait?
qa.a: Darshan kept every promise and made waiting fun by counting balls and singing, so Tanvir learned that waiting pays.

qa.q: How does Tanvir show his trust by March?
qa.a: He stands ready with pads on, counting balls under his breath, sure his turn will come.

grounding: A young cricket coach looks back on learning to keep small promises and make waiting fun, which taught a child that waiting pays.

passage:
Supervisor's note, community preschool, trainee placement.
Mohit, our twenty-year-old trainee, has had a noticeable effect on the four-year-olds, especially Hemant, who used to grab snacks before others were served and cry if made to wait.
What I observed: Mohit makes small promises and keeps every one. “After the story, the swings.” Then, after the story, the swings, every time. When the children must wait for snack, he leads a counting song: “Ten little mangoes on the tree…” and they count down together.
Last week, Hemant waited for all ten mangoes before reaching for his plate. Then he looked up at Mohit as if checking the promise would still hold. It did.
I think the reliability matters as much as the songs; the children have learned that waiting with Mohit actually pays.
What I did next: I asked Mohit to show the counting song to the other staff at Friday's meeting.

qa.q: What counting song does Mohit use?
qa.a: “Ten little mangoes on the tree.”

qa.q: What might Hemant have been feeling when he looked up at Mohit?
qa.a: He may have felt a little unsure and hopeful, checking whether the promise would hold, and then reassured when it did.

qa.q: Why is Mohit's approach effective?
qa.a: He keeps every small promise and gives children a song for waiting, so they learn that waiting is safe and pays.

qa.q: How might the other staff see Mohit's approach at Friday's meeting?
qa.a: They may feel curious and impressed, seeing that a simple song and reliable promises can calm grabbing and crying.

grounding: The supervisor's note shows a young trainee keeping small promises and using a counting song to help children learn to wait.

passage:
Thursday night.
Sachin is six and he used to scream if he had to wait even a minute. Since Ma started her night shifts, it's mostly me looking after him after college.
I've been trying two things. First, I only promise what I can actually do, and then I do it. If I say “one cartoon after homework,” he gets one cartoon after homework. No forgetting.
Second, when he has to wait, we sing. Today the pressure cooker needed three whistles before dinner. We sang “one whistle, two whistles” and clapped each one.
Tonight he waited for all three. He didn't cry. When I served the dal, he said, “You always do what you say, Mahi Didi.”
I had to turn around so he wouldn't see my eyes. I'm twenty and I'm tired. But this feels worth it.
— Mahima

qa.q: How many whistles did the pressure cooker need before dinner?
qa.a: It needed three whistles.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel when Sachin said “You always do what you say”?
qa.a: She felt deeply moved and a little tearful, turning away so he wouldn't see.

qa.q: What two things is Mahima doing to help Sachin wait?
qa.a: Keeping every small promise and singing during waits, which teaches him that waiting is reliable and bearable.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel now when he has to wait?
qa.a: Sachin seems calmer and trusting, since he knows his sister keeps her word.

grounding: The diary shows a young caregiver keeping small promises and using songs during waits, helping a child learn that waiting pays.

passage:
Bhavna was twenty and had been an anganwadi helper in Kothur for a year. At eleven every morning the children lined up for the single swing under the neem tree, and four-year-old Tejas always cried that his turn would never come.
Bhavna knelt in front of him. "After Priya, then you. I promise." Then she started a song, counting pushes: "Ek, do, teen..." Tejas sang along, and when they reached ten, Priya's turn ended. Bhavna lifted Tejas onto the swing, exactly as she had said.
She kept every small promise that way: a story after lunch, the red crayon after Meena. Some days it was hard, and she had to remember what she had said to whom.
By the end of the month, Tejas stood in the line singing the counting song by himself, and he did not cry.

qa.q: Where was the single swing?
qa.a: The single swing was under the neem tree.

qa.q: How does Tejas feel waiting for the swing by the end of the month?
qa.a: He feels calm and confident, singing the counting song himself instead of crying, because he trusts that his turn will really come.

qa.q: Which of Bhavna's habits helped Tejas, and why?
qa.a: She kept every small promise and gave him a counting song for the wait, which showed him that waiting pays off and gave him a way to fill the time.

qa.q: What is it like for Bhavna to keep all those small promises?
qa.a: It takes effort; some days are hard and she has to remember what she promised to whom, but she sees Tejas stop crying.

grounding: It shows a young caregiver keeping small promises and teaching a child to wait with a counting song, so the child learns waiting pays off.

passage:
Mei was nineteen, studying in Toronto and looking after her little brother Chen after school while their parents worked late at the restaurant. At first every wait was a fight. Chen screamed while the noodles boiled and kicked the door when she said "park later."
Mei changed two things. She stopped saying "later" unless she meant a time she could keep. "Park at five, after your reading," she would say, and at five they went, even in the snow. And while they waited, she gave him something to do. "Count the bubbles with me. Twenty, then noodles." They counted out loud, then sang the counting song their grandmother used to sing.
By February, Chen would stand by the stove counting on his own. One evening, when she was late tying her boots, he said, "It's fine, Jie-jie. I'll count to fifty."

qa.q: What did Mei say about the park after she changed her approach?
qa.a: She said, "Park at five, after your reading," and they went at five, even in the snow.

qa.q: How does Chen seem to feel about waiting by February?
qa.a: He seems calm and trusting, even offering to count to fifty when Mei is late, because he knows she keeps her word.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Vague "later" promises and empty waiting led to fights; keeping promises to set times and counting or singing together while waiting fixed it.

qa.q: How might their parents see the change when they come home from the restaurant?
qa.a: They would likely feel relieved and grateful to find a calmer Chen and less fighting in the evenings.

grounding: It shows a young caregiver keeping small promises and teaching a child to wait by counting and singing, so the child learns that waiting pays off.

passage:
Parul, twenty-one, was a trainee teacher at the municipal school, and Class 1 had one water tap for forty children. At the first break, Arohi pushed to the front every day, crying that the water would finish.
On Monday, Parul crouched beside her. "Arohi, you'll get water after Ravi. And at home time, I'll give you a star sticker if you wait. I promise."
Then she clapped a rhythm, and the children clapped back, counting each child who drank. Arohi clapped too, eyes on the tap.
At home time, Parul remembered. She peeled a star sticker onto Arohi's hand. Arohi looked at it as if it were gold.
Parul did the same every day that week, never forgetting, even on Friday when the principal was inspecting. By the next Monday, Arohi was clapping in the middle of the line, no pushing.

qa.q: How many children shared the one water tap?
qa.a: Forty children shared the one water tap.

qa.q: Why did Arohi look at the star sticker as if it were gold?
qa.a: She felt delighted and a little amazed that the promise was really kept, which made waiting feel worth it.

qa.q: What could other teachers learn from Parul's approach?
qa.a: They could keep small promises every time and give children a clapping or counting game to fill the wait, so patience is taught through reliability.

qa.q: How might the other children in line see Arohi by the next Monday?
qa.a: They would find her calmer and easier to line up with, clapping in the middle instead of pushing to the front.

grounding: It shows a young trainee teacher keeping small promises and using a clapping count to teach a child that waiting pays off.

passage:
Dear Professor Menon,
For my practicum report, here is what changed with Tejas, the four-year-old who used to scream whenever he had to wait for the swing.
In week one I noticed the grown-ups kept saying "in a minute" and then forgetting. So I made myself a rule: I only promise what I can keep, and I always keep it. If I said "after snack", it was after snack, every time.
I also gave him something to do while he waited. We sing "Five Little Ducks", one verse per turn, or count jumps on the spot to twenty. Yesterday he stood behind two children, singing to himself, and when his turn came he said, "I waited the whole song!"
He still cries some days. But I think he's learning that when I say wait, waiting pays.
Warm regards,
Gopika

qa.q: What song does Gopika sing with Tejas while he waits?
qa.a: "Five Little Ducks".

qa.q: How did Tejas feel when he said "I waited the whole song!"?
qa.a: Tejas seemed proud and pleased with himself, having managed a wait that used to make him scream.

qa.q: Which of Gopika's two changes mattered, and why?
qa.a: Keeping every small promise taught Tejas that "wait" means something real, and singing or counting gave him a way to fill the wait instead of just enduring it.

qa.q: What might waiting have felt like for Tejas when adults said "in a minute" and forgot?
qa.a: It probably felt pointless and upsetting, as if the turn might never come, so screaming made sense to him.

grounding: A trainee teacher keeps every small promise and teaches a child to wait by singing and counting, so he learns that waiting pays.
